The shared random effect $\alpha_i$ is what makes observations in the same group correlated.

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-re-cov}
#### Moments of the one-way random-effects model

Under @def-one-way-re, for any group $i$ and observations $j \neq k$:

$$
\ba
\E{Y_{ij}} &= \mu
\\
\Var{Y_{ij}} &= \sigma_\alpha^2 + \sigma^2
\\
\Cov{Y_{ij}, Y_{ik}} &= \sigma_\alpha^2
\ea
$$ {#eq-re-cov}

and observations in different groups are independent.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

This proof uses [the definition of covariance](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/variance-covariance.html#def-cov),
[the covariance of a variable with itself](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/variance-covariance.html#lem-cov-xx),
and linearity of expectation.

Mean:

$$
\ba
\E{Y_{ij}}
&= \E{\mu + \alpha_i + \epsilon_{ij}}
&& \text{(definition of the model)}
\\
&= \mu + \E{\alpha_i} + \E{\epsilon_{ij}}
&& \text{(linearity of expectation)}
\\
&= \mu + 0 + 0
&& \text{(both have mean zero)}
\\
&= \mu
&& \text{(simplify)}
\ea
$$ {#eq-re-cov-proof-1}

Covariance, for $j$ and $k$ equal or not:

$$
\ba
\Cov{Y_{ij}, Y_{ik}}
&\eqdef \E{(Y_{ij} - \mu)(Y_{ik} - \mu)}
&& \text{(definition of covariance)}
\\
&= \E{(\alpha_i + \epsilon_{ij})(\alpha_i + \epsilon_{ik})}
&& \text{(substitute the model)}
\\
&= \E{\alpha_i^2 + \alpha_i\epsilon_{ik} + \epsilon_{ij}\alpha_i + \epsilon_{ij}\epsilon_{ik}}
&& \text{(distribute)}
\\
&= \E{\alpha_i^2} + \E{\alpha_i\epsilon_{ik}} + \E{\epsilon_{ij}\alpha_i} + \E{\epsilon_{ij}\epsilon_{ik}}
&& \text{(linearity of expectation)}
\\
&= \sigma_\alpha^2 + \E{\alpha_i\epsilon_{ik}} + \E{\epsilon_{ij}\alpha_i} + \E{\epsilon_{ij}\epsilon_{ik}}
&& \text{($\E{\alpha_i} = 0$, so $\E{\alpha_i^2} = \Var{\alpha_i}$)}
\\
&= \sigma_\alpha^2 + 0 + 0 + \E{\epsilon_{ij}\epsilon_{ik}}
&& \text{(independent, mean-zero factors)}
\ea
$$ {#eq-re-cov-proof-2}

If $j \neq k$, $\epsilon_{ij}$ and $\epsilon_{ik}$ are independent with mean zero,
so $\E{\epsilon_{ij}\epsilon_{ik}} = 0$ and the covariance is $\sigma_\alpha^2$.
If $j = k$, $\E{\epsilon_{ij}^2} = \sigma^2$,
so the covariance of $Y_{ij}$ with itself,
which is its variance,
is $\sigma_\alpha^2 + \sigma^2$.

Observations in different groups $i \neq i'$
are functions of the disjoint sets of independent variables
$\{\alpha_i, \epsilon_{ij}\}$ and $\{\alpha_{i'}, \epsilon_{i'k}\}$,
so they are independent.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-dyestuff-cov}
#### Covariance between two dyestuff preparations

Suppose the batch-level variance in @exm-dyestuff is $\sigma_\alpha^2 = 1764$
and the within-batch variance is $\sigma^2 = 2451$.
Then by @thm-re-cov
two preparations from the same batch would have covariance $1764$,
and each preparation would have variance $1764 + 2451 = 4215$.
Two preparations from different batches would have covariance $0$.
:::
